title.en: Unit 10 · Infinite Sequences & Series — Convergence Tests

chapterTag.category: AP Calc BC BC-5 — Series Convergence

body.en: Unit 10 establishes the rigorous mathematical theory of infinite processes. Beginning with the formal (ε, N) definition of sequence limits, the unit develops the complete taxonomy of series convergence tests, proves the convergence of geometric series, and establishes the criteria for absolute versus conditional convergence.

blocks.heading: Level 1 · Foundations — Precise Sequence Limits & The Geometric Series Sum Proof

body.en: An infinite series \(\sum a_n\) is defined as the limit of its sequence of partial sums \(S_N = \sum_{n=1}^N a_n\). Understanding sequence convergence is the necessary prerequisite for series analysis.

label.en: ● Theorem & Formal Analytical Proof · Geometric Series Sum Formula

body.en:
Theorem: The geometric series \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty a r^n = a + ar + ar^2 + \dots\) converges if and only if \(|r| < 1\). When \(|r| < 1\), its infinite sum is: \[ S = \frac{a}{1 - r}. \] If \(|r| \ge 1\) and \(a \neq 0\), the series diverges.

Proof via Partial Sums: Consider the \(N\)-th partial sum: \[ S_N = a + ar + ar^2 + \dots + ar^{N-1}. \] Multiply both sides by the common ratio \(r\): \[ r S_N = ar + ar^2 + ar^3 + \dots + ar^N. \] Subtract the second equation from the first. All intermediate terms cancel in a telescoping subtraction: \[ S_N - r S_N = a - ar^N \implies S_N(1 - r) = a(1 - r^N). \] Since \(r \neq 1\), divide by \(1 - r\): \[ S_N = \frac{a(1 - r^N)}{1 - r}. \] Now take the limit as \(N \to \infty\): \[ S = \lim_{N\to\infty} S_N = \lim_{N\to\infty} \frac{a(1 - r^N)}{1 - r} = \frac{a}{1 - r}\left(1 - \lim_{N\to\infty} r^N\right). \] • If \(|r| < 1\), \(\lim_{N\to\infty} r^N = 0\), yielding: \[ S = \frac{a(1 - 0)}{1 - r} = \mathbf{\frac{a}{1 - r}}. \] • If \(|r| > 1\) or \(r = -1\), \(\lim_{N\to\infty} r^N\) does not exist (diverges).
• If \(r = 1\), \(S_N = N a \to \pm\infty\) as \(N \to \infty\). \(\blacksquare\)

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Unit 10 · Infinite Sequences & Series — Convergence Tests)

body.en:
Why the Geometric Sum Formula & \(S_\infty\) Work: Write \(S_n = a + ar + ar^2 + \dots + ar^{n-1}\). Multiplying through by \(r\) shifts every power up by one:

\[ S_n - rS_n = (a + ar + \dots + ar^{n-1}) - (ar + ar^2 + \dots + ar^n) = a - ar^n \]

Factoring \(S_n(1 - r) = a(1 - r^n)\) gives \(S_n = \dfrac{a(1 - r^n)}{1 - r}\) for \(r \ne 1\). Taking \(n \to \infty\), \(\lim_{n \to \infty} r^n = 0\) holds if and only if \(|r| < 1\), yielding \(S_\infty = \dfrac{a}{1 - r}\).

label.en: Level 1 (Foundations) — Worked Example · Geometric Series Identification & Sum

body.en:
Problem: Determine whether the series \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty 5\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)^n\) converges or diverges. If it converges, compute its exact sum.

Step 1 · Identify First Term \(a\) and Common Ratio \(r\):
• For \(n = 1\): \(a_1 = 5\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)^1 = -\frac{10}{3}\).
• The common ratio is \(r = -\frac{2}{3}\).

Step 2 · Convergence Test: \[ |r| = \left|-\frac{2}{3}\right| = \frac{2}{3} < 1. \] Since \(|r| < 1\), the geometric series converges.

Step 3 · Calculate Sum: \[ S = \frac{a_1}{1 - r} = \frac{-10/3}{1 - (-2/3)} = \frac{-10/3}{5/3} = -\frac{10}{3} \cdot \frac{3}{5} = \mathbf{-2}. \]

label.en: Worked Example \(B\) — Unit 10 · Infinite Sequences & Series — Convergence Tests (Hard Application)

body.en:
Problem (Hard): An arithmetic series \( \sum_{k=1}^{p} E_k \) has first term \( E_1 = 24 \) and common difference \( d = 8 \). What is the partial sum \( S_{8} \) for \( p = 8 \)?

Step-by-Step Solution: Using \( S_n = \frac{n}{2}(2a_1 + (n - 1)d) \), \( S_{8} = \frac{8}{2}(2(24) + 7(8)) = 416 \).

label.en: ⚠️ Common Exam Traps — Unit 10 · Infinite Sequences & Series — Convergence Tests

body.en:
1. Expanding \((a + bx)^n\) Without Factoring Out \(a^n\): For negative or fractional \(n\) on College Board AP Calculus BC, the formula \(1 + nu + \tfrac{n(n-1)}{2!}u^2 + \dots\) requires the first term inside the bracket to be 1: \((a + bx)^n = a^n\bigl(1 + \tfrac{b}{a}x\bigr)^n\). Omitting \(a^n\) loses almost all marks.

2. Confusing the \(n\)-th Term \(u_n\) with the Partial Sum \(S_n\): When given a formula for \(S_n\), extract \(u_n = S_n - S_{n-1}\) for \(n \ge 2\) and \(u_1 = S_1\).

body.en: Binomial Validity Shortcut (College Board AP Calculus BC): When asked for the range of \(x\) for which the expansion of \((a + bx)^n\) is valid, write \(\left|\dfrac{bx}{a}\right| < 1 \implies |x| < \left|\dfrac{a}{b}\right|\). blocks.heading: Level 2 · Medium — The Nine Series Convergence Tests Taxonomy

body.en: Every convergence problem on the AP Calculus BC exam can be resolved using one of nine standard tests. Knowing which test to apply and verifying its hypotheses is essential for scoring full justification points.

TestForm of SeriesConvergence ConditionDivergence Condition
1. \(n\)-th Term TestAny \(\sum a_n\)Never proves convergence\(\lim a_n \neq 0\)
2. Geometric Series\(\sum a r^n\)\(|r| < 1\) (Sum: \(\frac{a}{1-r}\))\(|r| \ge 1\)
3. \(p\)-Series Test\(\sum \frac{1}{n^p}\)\(p > 1\)\(p \le 1\) (Harmonic at \(p=1\))
4. Integral Test\(a_n = f(n) > 0\), decr.\(\int_1^\infty f(x)\,dx < \infty\)\(\int_1^\infty f(x)\,dx = \infty\)
5. Direct Comparison\(0 \le a_n \le b_n\)\(\sum b_n\) converges\(a_n \ge c_n\) and \(\sum c_n\) div.
6. Limit Comparison\(a_n, b_n > 0\)\(\lim \frac{a_n}{b_n} = L \in (0, \infty)\), \(\sum b_n\) conv.\(L \in (0, \infty)\), \(\sum b_n\) div.
7. Alternating Series (AST)\(\sum (-1)^{n+1} a_n\)\(a_n > 0\), decreases, \(\lim a_n = 0\)Use \(n\)-th term test
8. Ratio TestFactorials, powers\(\lim |\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}| = \rho < 1\)\(\rho > 1\) (Inconclusive if \(\rho = 1\))
9. Root Test\(n\)-th powers \((a_n)^n\)\(\lim \sqrt[n]{|a_n|} = \rho < 1\)\(\rho > 1\) (Inconclusive if \(\rho = 1\))

label.en: Level 2 (Medium) — Worked Example · Limit Comparison Test vs \(p\)-Series

body.en:
Problem: Determine the convergence or divergence of \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{3n^2 + 5}{2n^4 - n + 1}\).

Step 1 · Identify Dominant Terms: For large \(n\), \(a_n \approx \frac{3n^2}{2n^4} = \frac{3}{2n^2}\). Choose benchmark series \(b_n = \frac{1}{n^2}\).

Step 2 · State Benchmark Convergence: The series \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2}\) is a \(p\)-series with \(p = 2 > 1\), which converges.

Step 3 · Evaluate Limit of the Ratio: \[ L = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n} = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{\frac{3n^2 + 5}{2n^4 - n + 1}}{\frac{1}{n^2}} = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{3n^4 + 5n^2}{2n^4 - n + 1} = \frac{3}{2}. \]

Step 4 · Conclusion & Justification: Since \(L = \frac{3}{2}\) is finite and positive (\(0 < L < \infty\)), by the Limit Comparison Test, the series \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{3n^2 + 5}{2n^4 - n + 1}\) converges.

question.en:
Level 2 · Medium

Apply the Ratio Test to determine the convergence or divergence of \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{4^n}{n!}\).

solution.en: Set up the ratio: \[ \rho = \lim_{n\to\infty} \left| \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right| = \lim_{n\to\infty} \left| \frac{4^{n+1}}{(n+1)!} \cdot \frac{n!}{4^n} \right| = \lim_{n\to\infty} \left( \frac{4^{n+1}}{4^n} \cdot \frac{n!}{(n+1)n!} \right) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{4}{n+1} = 0. \] Since \(\rho = 0 < 1\), by the Ratio Test, the series converges absolutely.

blocks.heading: Level 3 · Advanced / AP FRQ — Absolute vs Conditional Convergence & Alternating Series Error

body.en: A series \(\sum a_n\) is conditionally convergent if \(\sum a_n\) converges, but \(\sum |a_n|\) diverges. On Free Response Question 6, students must rigorously prove convergence of the alternating series and bound truncation errors.

label.en: ● Theorem & Formal Analytical Proof · Absolute Convergence Implies Convergence

body.en:
Theorem: If \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty |a_n|\) converges, then \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\) converges.

Proof: For any real number \(a_n\), \(-|a_n| \le a_n \le |a_n|\). Adding \(|a_n|\) across all parts: \[ 0 \le a_n + |a_n| \le 2|a_n|. \] Since \(\sum |a_n|\) converges, \(\sum 2|a_n| = 2\sum |a_n|\) also converges. By the Direct Comparison Test, the series \(\sum (a_n + |a_n|)\) converges. Now express \(a_n\) as: \[ a_n = (a_n + |a_n|) - |a_n|. \] Since both \(\sum (a_n + |a_n|)\) and \(\sum |a_n|\) converge, their difference converges: \[ \sum a_n = \sum (a_n + |a_n|) - \sum |a_n|. \quad \blacksquare \]

Alternating Series Error Bound: If \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^{n+1} a_n\) satisfies the AST conditions (\(a_n > 0\), \(a_{n+1} \le a_n\), \(\lim a_n = 0\)), then: \[ |S - S_N| \le a_{N+1}. \]

label.en: Level 3 (Advanced/FRQ) — Worked Example · Absolute vs Conditional Convergence Justification

body.en:
Problem: Determine whether the alternating series \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n}{\sqrt{n}}\) converges absolutely, converges conditionally, or diverges.

Step 1 · Test Absolute Convergence: Consider the series of absolute values: \[ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left| \frac{(-1)^n}{\sqrt{n}} \right| = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^{1/2}}. \] This is a \(p\)-series with \(p = \frac{1}{2} \le 1\). Therefore, \(\sum |a_n|\) diverges. The series is NOT absolutely convergent.

Step 2 · Test the Original Alternating Series using AST: Check the three hypotheses of the Alternating Series Test:
1. Alternating sign: \((-1)^n\) oscillates signs.
2. Terms decrease in magnitude: \(a_n = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\). Since \(n + 1 > n \implies \sqrt{n+1} > \sqrt{n} \implies \frac{1}{\sqrt{n+1}} < \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\), terms strictly decrease.
3. Limit of terms: \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} = 0\).

All three hypotheses hold, so by the Alternating Series Test, the series \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n}{\sqrt{n}}\) converges.

Conclusion: Because the series converges but does not converge absolutely, it converges conditionally.

question.en:
Level 3 · Advanced / AP FRQ

The alternating series \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^4}\) converges to sum \(S\). If the sum is approximated by the fourth partial sum \(S_4\), use the Alternating Series Error Bound to find an upper bound for the error \(|S - S_4|\).

solution.en: The series satisfies the hypotheses of the AST: \(a_n = \frac{1}{n^4}\) is positive, strictly decreasing, and \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{n^4} = 0\). By the Alternating Series Error Bound: \[ |S - S_4| \le a_5 = \frac{1}{5^4} = \frac{1}{625} = \mathbf{0.0016}. \] The approximation error is guaranteed to be less than or equal to 0.0016.
